analysis.one_liner: Requires hazardous waste generators to treat, dispose of, or recycle their waste where it was created.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in January 1991 and died there when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any company that creates hazardous waste to treat it until harmless, or dispose of or recycle it, on the same site where the waste was generated. Small-quantity generators would be exempt. The idea is that waste should not be trucked across the country to landfills or disposal sites in other communities. It was introduced by one representative with no cosponsors and never moved beyond committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities near existing hazardous waste landfills, incinerators, and disposal facilities, which would receive less out-of-area waste, and neighborhoods along highway routes used to ship hazardous waste, which would see fewer waste shipments and fewer chances for spills. Communities near waste-generating factories would also see the waste treated or contained locally rather than shipped away.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near waste sites and shipping routes

how_it_helps.text: Each hazardous waste generator would have to treat its waste until harmless, or recycle or dispose of it, on the site where the waste was generated [S2][S3].
Companies that produce only small quantities of hazardous waste, as defined in the Solid Waste Disposal Act, would be exempt from the on-site requirement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Factories, chemical plants, and other generators of hazardous waste, which would have to build or run on-site treatment, disposal, or recycling capacity instead of paying commercial disposal firms to haul waste away — and, if those costs are passed on, consumers through higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hazardous waste generators and disposal companies

drawbacks.text: The bill leaves no room for the many existing, federally permitted commercial treatment and disposal facilities; forcing every generator to handle waste on its own site could be impractical for companies without the space or expertise, and would idle permitted facilities that in some cases are safer than improvised on-site handling [S3].

On-site disposal means hazardous waste stays where people live and work, shifting rather than reducing some local exposure risk, and the bill does not provide for how small industrial sites could handle land disposal restrictions under the existing hazardous waste law [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The idea addresses a real burden: hazardous waste is concentrated in a few communities chosen to receive other people's waste, and shipping it creates spill and accident risks along the way. But the bill is a blunt instrument — it bans the entire commercial disposal system with one line, exempts small generators whose aggregate waste is still significant, and offers no standards for on-site treatment. A designed version might have reduced interstate waste shipping while keeping regulated facilities as an option. As written, the cost to generators and disposal firms would have been large and the public-health benefit uncertain.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, then to its hazardous materials subcommittee a month later, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joseph Kolter introduced the bill on January 11, 1991 [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5].
On February 11, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Transportation and Hazardous Materials, where it remained [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hazardous waste generators and commercial waste disposal companies, which avoided the cost of on-site treatment and disposal and kept the existing waste-hauling system intact. Communities hosting disposal sites saw no change.

for.name: Rep. Joseph P. Kolter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; it never attracted a cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it; it was passed down to a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so no record shows where either party stood.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste treatment and disposal companies
industries.note: The bill would have barred generators from using commercial off-site treatment, disposal, and recycling services, eliminating most of the industry's core business. Companies in this industry profit by receiving waste shipped from generators nationwide, which is exactly what the bill would end.

industries.industry: Chemical, manufacturing, and other hazardous waste generators
industries.note: Large generators would have had to build or operate their own on-site treatment, disposal, or recycling instead of paying to have waste hauled away — a major compliance cost. The bill aimed that cost at them so communities near disposal sites would bear less.
